# Visa Gold Art Award

The Visa Gold Art Award was New Zealand's largest contemporary art prize during its existence, from 1991 to 1998.
History
The Visa Gold Art Award featured the works of the prize winners and selected finalists at both the Auckland Art Gallery and the City Gallery, Wellington, with the McDougall Contemporary Art Annex serving as the inaugural South Island location for the exhibition.
The Award was open to all New Zealand artists working in two-dimensional media, with the sole judging criterion being artistic merit. The overall victor received $15,000, while three merit prizes of $1,000 were given at the discretion of the judges. The panel in 1998 featured John McDonald, an art critic from the Sydney Morning Herald; Alexa Johnston, who was the principal curator at the Auckland Art Gallery; and John Reynolds, a New Zealand artist and winner of the 1993 Award.
The Award's inception dated back to when Visa began commissioning artwork for an advertising campaign. This proposal was transformed into a competition held at Wellington Polytechnic. By 1991, the Visa Gold Art Award had evolved into a national contest. In 1996, the final transformation of the Award occurred when entries were expanded to include two-dimensional media beyond just painting, incorporating photography and computer-generated images.
Winners
Recipients of the Visa Gold Art Award included some of New Zealand's most notable artists. In 1994, Luise Fong and Bill Hammond were announced as joint winners. Luise Fong won with her work Minor. Minor was later exhibited in the exhibition Cultural Safety: Contemporary Art from New Zealand, at Frankfurter Kunstverein in Germany (1995) and City Gallery Wellington in New Zealand (1995-1996). In 1995, Tony de Lautour took home the top prize. Fiona Pardington was the winner of the competition in 1997. Fiona Pardington previously won the Visa Gold Art Award in 1991 for Soft Target, a work framed with beaten, studded copper and gold-painted wood encrusted with contradictory religious images and texts.
Controversy
When Susan Jowsey won in 1996 with soiled clothing, people criticised her for having dirty laundry in a public space.
